Added in 4.6.0. `cmd/edge-relay` is a second binary, not a mode of the
Gateway: a poll-and-forward Sparkplug B edge node with no database, no web
UI, no auth and no write path. It exists to run on a Pi or a small industrial
PC at the edge, forwarding everything it reads to a full Gateway running
somewhere with a real database, over the same Sparkplug B publisher
(`internal/edgepublish`) 4.5.0 added.

4.5.0's own note said this directly: edge publish existed as a feature you
could turn on inside the full Gateway process, "not yet the standalone
lighter Edge Relay edition." This is that edition.

## What it is not

**Not a smaller Gateway with fewer options.** It is a different binary with a
different, much smaller set of dependencies. `cmd/edge-relay` never imports
`internal/store` (PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB), `internal/api` (the web UI and
auth), `internal/mcpserver`, `internal/mcpclient`, `internal/automation` or
`internal/entity` (the entity registry).
That is enforced by what the binary's own `main.go` imports, not by a flag, there is no `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_MODE` switch buried in the Gateway that turns
features off. The resulting binary is roughly a third of the size of the
Gateway's (12.5 MB vs. 33.9 MB on amd64, 11.7 MB vs. 31.6 MB on arm64,
`CGO_ENABLED=0`, both stripped, measured from the images this repository's
Containerfiles build). And it is checked:
`TestEdgeRelayDoesNotImportGatewayOnlyPackages` asks `go list -deps` what the
binary actually links, and fails if any of those packages creeps in through a
shared one.

**Not able to serve a UI, take a write, or answer an MCP tool call.** All
three need something this binary deliberately does not have: an
authenticated identity to attribute the action to. An edge relay decides
nothing and confirms nothing back to a human; it reads and forwards.

**Not configured through a database, and it has no config API of its own.**
Devices and tags come from a local JSON file read at startup, or from a file
the Gateway pushes over the broker, which applies live (see
[Config push](#config-push-480)). Nothing listens on the relay
for a new config: the only way in is the broker connection it already dials
out on.

## How it fits together

Internally this reuses the Gateway's actual polling engine
(`internal/runtime`), not a reimplementation of it: the same worker,
reconnect/backoff, and poll-loop code that has run in production as part of
the Gateway runs here unchanged. What differs is *where configuration and
history go*. `internal/runtime.Manager` talks to a `Backend` interface, `EnabledDevices`, `Tags`, `WriteHistory`, and so on, that `internal/store.Store`
already satisfied without any change of its own. `internal/edgerelay.Backend`
is the other implementation: devices and tags come from the JSON file instead
of Postgres, history-writing is a no-op (this binary forwards instead of
storing), and the system-log calls the Gateway would send to a database table
become a structured log line instead.

Everything downstream of a poll, the driver, the tag bus, the Sparkplug
publisher, the on-disk forward queue, is the exact same code the Gateway
uses when `HOTLOOP_EDGE_PUBLISH_ENABLED` is set. See `docs/EDGE-PUBLISH.md` for
what that publisher actually does: births, sequence numbers, buffering
through an outage, replay on reconnect. None of that changed here; this
binary is a different way of arriving at the same `Offer()` call.

## The device file

```json
{
  "devices": [
    {
      "id": "press-01",
      "name": "Press 1",
      "protocol": "opcua",
      "address": "opc.tcp://press-01.local:4840",
      "enabled": true,
      "pollIntervalMs": 1000
    }
  ],
  "tags": [
    {
      "deviceId": "press-01",
      "name": "Zone1_Temp",
      "address": "ns=2;s=Zone1.Temp",
      "dataType": "float",
      "enabled": true
    }
  ]
}
```

A tag takes everything the Gateway's tags do, `noData` included: a list of
raw values that mean "no measurement" (a recorder's 0x8005), each with a
reason, so a dead channel reads bad on the relay and in the Sparkplug stream
instead of as a number. See [No-data values](/iot/protocols/#no-data-values).

Same `Device` and `Tag` JSON shapes the Gateway's own API accepts, see
`internal/model/device.go`, validated with the identical rules (a device
needs a known protocol, a tag needs a device that exists), plus two checks a
single file can get wrong that a database's own constraints would have
caught: a device id declared twice, and a tag pointing at a device that was
never declared.

All seven of the Gateway's protocol drivers are compiled in: OPC UA, Modbus,
MQTT/Sparkplug B, EtherNet/IP, S7comm, MTConnect and HTTP. Nothing about the
device file format is edge-relay-specific.

### Discovery (4.18.10)

A relay can listen to an MQTT broker for devices that announce themselves, the
way the Gateway does (see [DISCOVERY.md](/iot/mqtt-discovery/)), and read and forward
whatever it hears. Name the brokers in the device file:

```json
{
  "devices": [],
  "tags": [],
  "discovery": [
    {
      "id": "yard",
      "broker": "10.0.0.5:1883",
      "username": "hotloop",
      "password": "...",
      "prefix": "homeassistant",
      "listenOnly": true,
      "tasmota": true,
      "shelly": true
    }
  ]
}
```

`id` is 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits and `-`, and not `embedded`. `broker`,
`username`, `password`, `useTls` and `insecureSkipVerify` are what the
Gateway's Settings, MQTT take, checked by the same code. `prefix` defaults to
`homeassistant`, and `tasmota` and `shelly` to on. A file that names no broker
changes nothing about how a relay runs.

What it hears becomes devices and tags, made by the same code the Gateway
runs (the `homeassistant/` format, Tasmota's own, Shelly's statuses), and they
are polled and forwarded over Sparkplug like any other. A device's id is made
from the broker's id and who the device says it is, the same every time
(`disc-<identity>-<hash>`), so a relay that restarts names its metrics the
same. A device appears a couple of seconds after it announces, a withdrawn one
leaves the node's birth in a rebirth, and neither costs the Sparkplug session or the forward queue. A
pushed file that adds or removes a broker applies live too.

**Nothing it discovers can be armed.** Not because a check says so. Every tag
discovery makes is read-only, as it is on the Gateway; every device it makes is
not accepted; there is nobody on a relay to accept one; and a relay has no write
path at all, so a command to a discovered point, or to any point, is refused
before it gets near a device. The test for it asks a relay with writes allowed
to switch a discovered pump, and checks the pump's command topic stayed quiet.

A device you can command reaches a relay the other way round: you accept it on a
Gateway, arm the points you mean to, and push the file. When a file has a
device the relay also hears (the same broker id, or the same address, and the
same identity), the file's wins and the discovered copy is not made, so one
device is never forwarded twice.

`listenOnly` is on unless you turn it off, and then the relay publishes nothing
to that broker: not the birth message that makes a publisher announce itself
again, not a Shelly's `status_update`, not a Tasmota's power query. A device
that only speaks when it changes reads unknown until it does. Turn it off
and those are the only things it sends, to the topics DISCOVERY.md names.

A relay keeps nothing about what it heard. The `homeassistant/` and Tasmota
configs are retained on their broker and come back when it starts; a Shelly
says its statuses whenever something changes, so a device that has been quiet
since the relay started is not there until it speaks. That, and not having a
database to remember a device accepted in, is the difference from the Gateway.

`/status` says, under `discovery`, for each broker: whether it is listening and
connected, how many messages it received, dropped and refused, and how many
problems are on it, and the number of devices and tags discovery made. It does
not say where a broker is, or what topic a problem was on.

### Credentials in the device file (4.15.0)

The relay's OPC UA driver is the Gateway's, so a device can carry an OPC UA
`username` and `password` (and the security options in
[PROTOCOLS.md](/iot/protocols/#opc-ua-security-and-credentials)) in its `config`
block, and so can a device of any other protocol (MQTT and HTTP passwords, HTTP
headers, credentials in an address). Those are in the device file in the clear, and
the relay has no API to hide them behind (the API redaction added to the Gateway
in 4.15.1 does not apply to it; see
[AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/#where-credentials-are-still-in-the-clear)), so where the file
lives matters:

- **In the Helm chart, use `devicesSecret`.** Devices set in the chart's `devices`
  and `tags` values are rendered into a ConfigMap, which anyone allowed to read
  ConfigMaps in the namespace can read, and they are kept in the Helm release
  record. For devices with credentials, put the whole device file in a Secret
  under the key `devices.json` and name it in `devicesSecret`; the Secret is
  mounted in place of the ConfigMap, which is then not created.
- **A pushed device file carries them too.** A file pushed with `POST
  /api/fleet/{id}/config` is published, retained, to an MQTT topic, so the broker
  must carry TLS and restrict who may read `hotloop/edge-relay-config/#`, or
  whoever can subscribe to it can read every credential in it. The relay writes a
  pushed file with mode `0600`, on its data volume (`/data/pushed-devices.json`
  in the chart and the Quadlet unit), so it's on the PVC too, not in a Secret.
- **A secured OPC UA device keeps a certificate and a trust store.** They live
  under `/data/opcua-client-pki` (`HOTLOOP_OPCUA_CLIENT_PKI_DIR`), on the same
  persistence volume as the forward queue. With the chart's persistence off
  that's an emptyDir, so every new pod makes a new certificate and every
  secured server has to trust it again (see "Persistence off" below); an
  anonymous device on an unsecured channel doesn't care. Approving a server's certificate is the same move as on the
  Gateway, `rejected/` to `trusted/`, done on the relay's volume.

## Remote commands (4.7.0)

Two Sparkplug NCMD commands, both over the same connection this relay
already dials out on, no inbound connection required:

- **Rebirth** (`Node Control/Rebirth`), since 4.5.0, via
  `internal/edgepublish`.
- **Restart** (`Node Control/Reboot`), since 4.7.0: the relay publishes its
  own graceful NDEATH and exits, relying on its supervisor (a Quadlet unit's
  `Restart=always`, or a Deployment's default `restartPolicy: Always`) to
  bring it back up.

- **Update** (`Node Control/Update`): an operator approving the image update a
  relay is holding for. It only does anything to a relay set to hold updates;
  see [Updating a relay](#updating-a-relay).

Nothing on the relay's own side decides who is allowed to send these, see
`docs/FLEET.md` for the Gateway-side fleet manager that sends them, and the
broker ACL requirement that is the actual authorization boundary.

## Updating a relay

A relay is not updated by the Gateway. It can't be: the Gateway has no way
onto the box, and the relay can't replace its own container, so "remote
update" means different things for the two ways to install one, and this page
says which, because a promise the platform can't keep is worse than none.

**The rule is the one every HotLoop box follows: track `:stable`, never pin.**
A relay pinned to `4.17.0` is exactly as old as the day somebody installed it,
and nobody remembers to go back to a plant floor and bump it. So the image a
relay follows is `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge-relay:stable`, and every
release moves that tag. What differs is who restarts the relay onto it.

### Quadlet (a Pi or a small industrial PC): it updates itself

The unit in [`deploy/quadlet`](/install/quadlet/) follows `:stable`
and carries the label Podman's auto-update looks for. Turn the timer on once
per box:

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
```

When the timer fires, Podman pulls `:stable`, and if the digest changed it
restarts the unit on the new image. Three things make that safe to leave
alone, and all three were proven by running them, not by reading about them:

- **A relay that can't come back is put back.** The unit has a healthcheck
  (`/edge-relay --healthcheck`, because the image has no shell or curl to run
  one) and tells systemd it isn't up until that passes. If the new image never
  does, Podman moves the previous image back under `:stable` and starts that
  one. A release that can't start costs a few minutes on one box, not a relay
  that stays down. On Podman 4.9 (Ubuntu 24.04) `Notify=healthy` alone does
  not do this: it is read as plain `true`, the relay is called up the moment
  its container starts, and Podman reports the update a success while the
  relay is dead. The unit sets `--sdnotify=healthy` explicitly for that
  reason.
- **The Gateway sees every update.** A relay puts its version and the digest
  of its image in every birth. The Gateway's fleet list shows both per relay,
  and writes a line to the system log when one changes: what it was, what it
  is now, and both digests. That is the audit trail, and it covers an update
  from any cause, including an operator on the box.
- **An update leaves the data alone.** The forward queue and a pushed device
  file live on the data volume, which a new image doesn't touch. What is lost
  is the polling while the relay restarts, a few seconds at most.

The digest a relay reports is what `podman image inspect --format
'{{.Digest}}'` prints on that box, which is the thing auto-update follows.
Podman can know one image by more than one digest (it lists them under
`RepoDigests`) when a registry stores a different manifest format than the one
it works with, so compare it the same way on every relay, not against a
registry's header.

### Quadlet, holding updates until an operator approves (opt-in)

Some sites would rather say when: a relay on a line that can't blink during a
shift. That is `edge-relay-hold.conf`,
a systemd drop-in, and it is never the default. With it the relay reports
`"updateMode": "approve"`, the timer is off, and nothing updates until an admin
sends `POST /api/fleet/{id}/update` from the Gateway. The relay then exits with
status 75, systemd starts it again on the image it has, and a separate job
waits for it to be healthy and runs `podman auto-update`: the new image if
there is one, with the same rollback, and a relay that blinked for nothing if
there isn't. Proven with a real update held for 30 seconds while the relay ran
untouched, then taken on approval.

Know what it costs. The timer has to be off for the whole machine, because
Podman's auto-update acts on every labeled container and can't be told to skip
one; a box that has to run it for other things can't hold this relay. And the
Gateway can't tell you an update is waiting, only what each relay runs now, so
compare the fleet list with what `:stable` is before you approve. An approval
carries no image: the relay can only be told to update to what its own unit
follows.

### Helm: you run `helm upgrade`

A pod can't replace itself, and a Deployment is Helm's to change, so there is
no remote update for the chart. The chart's `image.tag` defaults to its
`appVersion`, which is the release, so:

```sh
helm repo update
helm upgrade edge-relay hotloop/hotloop-edge-relay --reuse-values
```

rolls the pod onto the new release. The chart's strategy stops the old pod
before it starts the new one (`maxSurge: 0`, because the forward queue is a
single-writer file on one volume), so there is a gap while it comes up. The Gateway still sees the new version in the
relay's next birth and logs the change. Under Helm a relay doesn't report an
image digest (a container can't see its own, and Kubernetes doesn't hand it
down), only its version. `Node Control/Update` does nothing here and the relay
says so in its log; Helm is the approval.

### What is not here, and why

- **Signed images and a digest allowlist.** The Gateway can't enforce either
  on a box it has no way onto, and a check the relay runs on itself is one
  that a compromised relay skips. Podman can verify signatures at pull time
  (`policy.json`), which is the place that works; nothing here sets that
  policy up for you, and `:stable` is trusted the way any tag is.
- **Staged rollout.** Every relay on a box follows the same tag on its own
  timer, so a fleet updates over the timer's spread, not in waves, and the
  rollback above is what limits a bad release. To stage deliberately, hold the
  sites that should wait with the hold drop-in and approve them in the order
  you want.

## Config push (4.8.0)

A new device file can be pushed on a separate, plain (non-Sparkplug),
retained MQTT topic. See `docs/FLEET.md`'s "Config push" section for the
Gateway's side. Up to 4.17 a push only staged the file and the relay kept
polling the old list until something restarted it. That made every change to
what a relay polls a restart of the relay, its broker session and every
device session it held, on a box that is supposed to sit there for months
without being touched. Now a push applies the moment it lands.

- Pushed while this relay is **running**: the bytes are validated with the
  same rules `LoadDeviceFile` applies at boot, saved to
  `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_PUSHED_FILE` (or over `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_DEVICES_FILE`
  when that isn't set; see below), and applied live. Saved first, on
  purpose: a list that ran but was never saved would quietly revert at the
  next boot.
- **A bad push is refused and the old list keeps running.** One that won't
  parse, won't validate (a duplicate device, a tag on a device nobody
  declared, an unknown protocol) or can't be saved changes nothing: not the
  running devices, not the file on disk. The log says why, and so does
  `/status` under `config.rejected`, which is where the Gateway's fleet
  screen picks it up.
- Pushed while this relay was **offline**: nothing is there to receive it
  until the next boot, at which point the relay gives a retained push a
  couple of seconds to arrive *before* it loads its local device file (see
  `applyPushedConfig` in `cmd/edge-relay/main.go`), so it boots straight
  into it. A push that shows up after those two seconds applies live like
  any other.
- The broker hands the retained push back on every reconnect. The relay
  knows the file it's running by its sha256, so the same bytes arriving
  again change nothing.

### What a live apply keeps, and what it changes

The relay works out what changed between the file it's running and the new
one, device by device, and touches only that:

- **A device that didn't change keeps its session.** Same TCP connection to
  the PLC, same OPC UA subscription, no gap in its readings.
- **A changed device** (its address, protocol, poll interval, timeout,
  config block or tags) is reconnected with the new definition.
- **A new device** is connected and starts polling.
- **A removed device** (or one now `"enabled": false`) is disconnected.
- **The Sparkplug session stays up.** No NDEATH, no reconnect, same bdSeq,
  and the forward queue isn't touched. A reload during a broker outage
  leaves every buffered reading in the queue; they drain when the broker is
  back, the same as without a reload.

On the wire, per Sparkplug B. The relay is one edge node and every tag is a
node metric named `device/tag`, so the node's metric set is what changes, and
Sparkplug gives a node exactly one way to change it: a new NBIRTH, which
replaces the last one whole. So:

- **Metrics that went away** (a removed device, a removed or disabled tag)
  are sent once more in an NDATA as null, then the node rebirths without
  them: same session, same bdSeq, seq back to 0, the same rebirth a
  `Node Control/Rebirth` gets. The null is there because a host is allowed
  to keep the last value of a metric a new birth leaves out, and the
  Gateway's own Sparkplug host does exactly that. Without the null, a valve
  you took off the relay would sit on its last good reading forever,
  looking healthy.
- **Metrics that are new** go into a birth on their device's first poll, the
  same way every metric does at boot. A birth never names a metric before
  there's a reading behind it.
- **Readings of a removed tag still in the forward queue** are dropped when
  the queue drains, with a log line counting them. The node's birth no
  longer carries that metric, and Sparkplug has no legal way to send one it
  doesn't, so sending them would mean an alias no host was ever told about.

Editing the local device file by hand still takes a restart: the relay reads
it at boot and when a push is cleared, and doesn't watch it. Under the chart
that's what a `helm upgrade` changing `devices` does anyway.

### Where a pushed file lives, and which file wins

Both supported installs mount the local device file read-only: the chart from
a ConfigMap (or Secret), the Quadlet unit as a `:ro` bind, and both on a
read-only root filesystem. Up to 4.16.0 the relay wrote a push right next to
that file, so on either install every single push died with

```
a pushed config was rejected; keeping the current one and continuing to run
error="write /etc/edge-relay/devices.json.tmp: open /etc/edge-relay/devices.json.tmp: read-only file system"
```

and the relay kept polling the old list. The Gateway said `config pushed`, the
restart went through, and nothing changed. That's fixed by giving the push its
own home:

- **`HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_PUSHED_FILE`** is where a push is written. The chart
  sets it to `/data/pushed-devices.json` on the PVC (`pushedDevicesFile` in
  values.yaml), and the Quadlet unit sets the same path on its named data
  volume. Both outlive the container, and the PVC outlives a reschedule. That
  last part is deliberate: an emptyDir would be writable too, but it's gone
  the moment the pod moves, and a relay that silently goes back to its old
  device list after a node drain is the same bug with extra steps.
- **The pushed file wins.** At boot the relay loads the pushed file if it
  exists, and the local one only if it doesn't. That holds after a restart,
  after a reschedule, after the broker has lost the retained push (a
  Mosquitto restart without persistence), and after a `helm upgrade` that
  changes `devices` or `tags`. The push is the newer, deliberate change, and
  the broker would hand the retained copy straight back at the next boot
  anyway, so letting the local file win would only last one restart. The
  first lines of the log say which file it booted from:
  `booting from the pushed device file; the local one is ignored until the
  push is cleared`.
- **Going back to the local file** (the chart's `devices`, or
  `/etc/edge-relay/devices.json` under Quadlet) is `DELETE
  /api/fleet/{id}/config` on the Gateway. The delete clears the retained push
  on the broker, so no later boot applies it, and a relay that's connected at
  the time loads its local file, deletes its pushed file, logs `the config
  push was cleared; the local device file takes over`, and applies the local
  file live, the same way a push applies. If the local file doesn't load, the
  relay keeps the pushed file running and on disk and says so in the log and
  in `/status`: deleting it first would leave a relay that boots into a
  broken file at its next restart. Fix the local file and send the delete
  again. Do it while the relay is **online**. A clear isn't retained, so a
  relay that was offline for it never hears about it and keeps its pushed
  file; bring it up and send the delete again. It's safe to repeat.
- A pushed file that exists but won't load (a disk fault, or a later release
  with stricter rules) is logged as an error and the relay boots from the
  local file rather than staying down over it.
- With `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_PUSHED_FILE` unset, a push overwrites
  `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_DEVICES_FILE` itself, the 4.8.0 behavior. That's only
  any good for a bare binary with a writable device file, and then there's no
  separate copy for a clear to drop.

If a push "didn't take", look at the relay's log before anything else. Either
it says which file it booted from, or it says why the push was rejected.

## The HTTP surface

Two endpoints, both unauthenticated, both read-only:

- `GET /healthz`, the process is up. Nothing more; a device being
  disconnected is not this process being unhealthy.
- `GET /status`, a snapshot: device counts by connection state, tag count,
  the forward queue's current depth, the compiled-in protocol list, and
  `uplink`: whether the broker is connected, whether a replay is running,
  and what the forward queue holds, weighs on disk and has dropped at its
  bound (see docs/EDGE-PUBLISH.md, "When the uplink is down"). No
  tag values, no device addresses, no configuration, this is a monitoring
  surface, not a smaller copy of the Gateway's dashboard. `version`,
  `imageDigest` and `updateMode` say what build it is and whether it holds
  updates. It also says which
  device file is running, under `config`: `source` (`local` or
  `pushed`), `path`, its sha256 `digest`, `appliedAt`, and `rejected`, the
  last file the relay refused and why, until a push after it applies. The
  digest, not the file: the Gateway can match it against what it pushed
  without the file's addresses and credentials going out on an
  unauthenticated port. With a `discovery` broker in the file it also says,
  under `discovery`, how each one is doing and how many devices it found (see
  Discovery).

Deliberately no auth in front of either: an edge relay has no user database,
no session store and no identity system to build one from, and adding a
single shared token would be theatre rather than security for two endpoints
that expose nothing sensitive. Run it behind whatever network perimeter the
device itself sits behind, the same expectation the Gateway's own
`auth.insecure` mode already documents for a deployment behind a trusted
proxy.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_DEVICES_FILE` | n/a | Required. Path to the device file above |
| `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_PUSHED_FILE` | unset | Where a pushed device file is kept, and it wins over the one above while it exists. Must be writable and persistent; the chart and the Quadlet unit use `/data/pushed-devices.json`. See [Where a pushed file lives](#where-a-pushed-file-lives-and-which-file-wins) |
| `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_LISTEN_ADDR` | `:8081` | The `/healthz` and `/status` server |
| `HOTLOOP_EDGE_RELAY_UPDATE_MODE` | `auto` | `auto` leaves updating to the supervisor and ignores an approval from the Gateway; `approve` holds updates until one arrives. See [Updating a relay](#updating-a-relay) |
| `HOTLOOP_IMAGE_DIGEST` | unset | The digest of the image this relay runs from, as its supervisor knows it. The Quadlet unit sets it before every start. Reported in `/status` and every birth; empty is fine |
| `HOTLOOP_LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | |
| `HOTLOOP_POLL_INTERVAL` | `5s` | Default poll interval; a device's own `pollIntervalMs` overrides it |
| `HOTLOOP_MIN_POLL_INTERVAL` | `100ms` | Floor enforced on every device, regardless of its own setting |
| `HOTLOOP_POLL_TIMEOUT` | `10s` | Default per-poll timeout; a device's own `timeoutMs` overrides it |
| `HOTLOOP_MAX_CONCURRENT_POLLS` | `32` | Devices that may be mid-poll at once |
| `HOTLOOP_RECONNECT_MIN` / `HOTLOOP_RECONNECT_MAX` | `1s` / `60s` | Backoff bounds between reconnect attempts, jittered |
| `HOTLOOP_RING_SIZE` | `120` | Samples per tag kept for `/status`-adjacent diagnostics |
| `HOTLOOP_OPCUA_CLIENT_PKI_DIR` | `/data/opcua-client-pki` | The OPC UA driver's certificate and its `trusted/` and `rejected/` stores; a device's own `pkiDir` overrides it. Only a secured OPC UA device touches it |

Identical variable names and defaults to the Gateway's own `RuntimeConfig`, see its "Polling" section in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` for the same settings
expressed as Helm values, because both binaries load this config through
the same `config.LoadRuntimeConfig()` function, not two copies that could
drift apart.

Plus every `HOTLOOP_EDGE_PUBLISH_*` variable `docs/EDGE-PUBLISH.md` documents,
with one difference: `HOTLOOP_EDGE_PUBLISH_ENABLED` is ignored and forwarding is
always on, publishing what it reads is this binary's entire purpose, not an
opt-in feature the way it is on the Gateway.

## What has and has not been verified

Tested end to end against a real Mosquitto broker and a real polled device (an
`httptest` HTTP endpoint standing in for the plant): a reading crosses the
poll loop, the tag bus, and the Sparkplug publisher, and arrives at a plain
MQTT subscriber as a decoded, correctly-valued NDATA, the same test shape
`internal/edgepublish`'s own suite uses, run here through the whole binary's
actual wiring rather than against the publisher in isolation.

Live reload is tested the same way, against Modbus TCP slaves on real
sockets, the lab's opc-plc, a real Mosquitto, and the Gateway's own
Sparkplug host driver reading what the relay publishes
(`internal/edgerelay/reload_test.go`). One change adds an OPC UA device,
removes a Modbus one, changes another and leaves a fourth alone, and the
test checks: no NDEATH and the same bdSeq on every birth after it; the
removed metric nulled before the rebirth that drops it, and the host showing
it bad, not stuck on its last value; the new and changed tags reaching the
host with good values; the untouched device keeping its TCP session to its
slave; and no NDATA ever naming an alias its birth didn't announce. A second
test applies a change while the broker is cut off and readings are piling up,
and checks the whole queue drains afterwards with the removed device's
readings dropped, not sent. The compiled binary is tested too, as a
subprocess: a push applies in the same process, and a bad push leaves the
running list, the file on disk and `/status` saying why.

Discovery is tested the same way (`internal/edgerelay/discovery_test.go`,
`internal/discovery/scout_test.go`). A sensor announced on a real broker is
found by a running relay and its value read by the Gateway's Sparkplug host
driver from the relay's own output; a device withdrawn is retired from the
node's birth in a rebirth, with no NDEATH; a pushed file adds and removes a
broker live; and a relay with writes allowed is asked to switch a discovered
pump, and refuses, with nothing on the pump's command topic. The part that turns
announcements into devices is held to the Gateway's: every recording of every
publisher in `internal/discovery/testdata` (Zigbee2MQTT, ESPHome, Tasmota,
Shelly) is fed through both the Gateway's discovery on a real store and a
broker, and the Scout the relay uses, and they must end up with the same
devices carrying the same tags. They do. What that rests on is those recordings
and the maker's documentation, the same as on the Gateway, and no device on a
bench.

**Not yet run against real EtherNet/IP or S7comm hardware in this
configuration**: those drivers are the same, already-tested code the Gateway
uses (see each protocol's own section in `docs/PROTOCOLS.md`). OPC UA and
Modbus have been through the relay end to end in the live reload tests
above. **Not yet run against a certified Sparkplug host application**, the
same gap `docs/EDGE-PUBLISH.md` names for the Gateway's own edge-publish
feature, this binary publishes through the identical code path, so it
inherits that gap rather than adding a new one.

## Deploying it

Two supported paths, both containers, no bare `podman run`
invoked from a shell that dies with the session, and no Docker:

- **`charts/hotloop-edge-relay`**, a k3s Helm chart, separate from
  the Gateway's own chart (`charts/hotloop`), since an edge relay is
  a genuinely different artifact that often runs in a different, smaller
  cluster than the Gateway it forwards to. Devices and tags are declared in
  `values.yaml` and rendered into a ConfigMap; the forward queue lives on a
  small PVC (see "Persistence off" below before you turn that off).
- **`deploy/quadlet`**, a Podman Quadlet unit for a Pi or a small industrial
  PC that is not part of a k3s cluster at all. Quadlet turns the container
  into a real systemd service: starts on boot, restarts on failure, logs to
  journald, see that directory's own README for install steps.

Both use the same image (`Containerfile.edge-relay`, built and proven in CI) and
the same environment variables documented above.

Every release publishes both, from 4.16.0 on. The image is
`ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge-relay`, tagged with the release version (plus
`major.minor`, `major`, `latest` and `stable`; the Quadlet unit follows
`stable`, see [Updating a relay](#updating-a-relay)). It's amd64 and arm64, and 32-bit arm
(arm/v7) from the first release after 4.17.0, because a Pi 3 or a 32-bit Pi OS
install is exactly the box a relay ends up on. The chart is in the same Helm
repository as the Gateway's:

```sh
helm repo add hotloop https://hotloop.io/hotloop/
helm install edge-relay hotloop/hotloop-edge-relay \
  --namespace hotloop --create-namespace \
  --set edgePublish.broker=tcp://gateway.example.local:1883 \
  --set edgePublish.group=Plant1
```

### Persistence off

`persistence.enabled=false` gets you a relay that runs with no PVC, and
exactly that. On 4.16.0 it didn't even run: nothing was mounted at `/data`,
the root is read-only, and the relay died at boot with `open forward queue at
/data/forward.db: no such file or directory`. Now `/data` is an emptyDir,
capped at `persistence.size`, and everything the relay writes lands there.

An emptyDir lives as long as the pod. A container restart inside the same pod
keeps it. A new pod doesn't, and you get a new pod on a node drain, a node
dying, an eviction, a `kubectl delete pod`, and any `helm upgrade` that rolls
the Deployment. Each time, you lose:

- **The forward queue.** Every reading buffered while the broker was down is
  gone, and nothing on the Gateway side knows it's missing.
- **A pushed device file.** The relay boots from the chart's `devices` again
  without complaint, until the Gateway pushes again or the broker replays a
  retained push. That's the exact failure the PVC is there to prevent, and
  turning it off opts you back into it.
- **The OPC UA client certificate and trust store.** Every secured server has
  to trust the new certificate, and the operator has to approve every server's
  certificate again.

Filling the cap, which a queue set unbounded (`queueMaxBytes: 0`; the default
is 64 MiB) will do in a
long enough outage, gets the pod evicted and loses all three at once. That's
still better than filling the node's disk under everything else on it. The
install notes print a warning when persistence is off. It's fine for a trial.
For a relay whose readings matter, give it the PVC.

### From the EmberNet App Store

The store lists the relay as HotLoop Edge Relay, one per node. A store deploy
hands the chart three things: the display name (the release name), a node
selector, and the tenant labels. It has no form to ask for anything else, and
the relay can't run without a broker and a Sparkplug group. So a store deploy
of the relay stops at the render, on purpose, with an error in the helm-install
job's log that names what's missing and prints the exact command to fix it.

We didn't give it a default broker, because there isn't one that's true for
anybody's plant, and a relay pointed at a made-up address would look deployed
while it forwards nothing. It can't sit and wait for a pushed device file
either: a push arrives over the broker connection it doesn't have yet.

The fix is to put the two values into what the store wrote, and the install
retries by itself:

```sh
# a node on the local cluster: add them under spec.valuesContent
kubectl -n default edit helmchart hotloop-edge-relay-<node>

# a tenant on its own cluster (Fleet): add them under spec.helm.values
kubectl -n fleet-default edit helmop hotloop-edge-relay-<node>
```

```yaml
edgePublish:
  broker: tcp://<gateway-or-broker>:1883
  group: <sparkplug group id>
```

Once it's up it shows in Running Apps under the name the store gave it, with
the HotLoop icon, scoped to the tenant that deployed it, and no LAUNCH button.
That last part is deliberate: the chart labels it `embernet.ai/gui-type: none`,
because `/healthz` and `/status` are for a probe and an operator's curl, not a
page in an iframe.

The relay and the Gateway share a version number. A release won't start unless
both charts carry the tag's version and the relay's Quadlet unit follows
`:stable`, so the relay gets a new version every release whether its own code
changed or not. That's on purpose: one number to ask about, and no relay chart
pointing at a relay image nobody pushed. The Quadlet unit used to pin the
release number, which is the opposite of how a box that updates itself works.
